enonce_markdown: The list 7, 3, 9, 2 is to be sorted into ascending order with bubble sort. What does the list contain after the first complete pass from left to right?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In one bubble-sort pass, each pair of neighbours is compared from left to right and swapped if the left one is bigger. The largest value ends in the last place.

### Solution

Compare 7 and 3: swap, giving 3, 7, 9, 2. Compare 7 and 9: no swap. Compare 9 and 2: swap, giving 3, 7, 2, 9. After pass 1 the list is **3, 7, 2, 9**. A full sort needs more passes, so option b is wrong.

enonce_markdown: Which sorting algorithm works by repeatedly finding the smallest item in the unsorted part of the list and moving it to the front of that part?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Each sorting algorithm is named after its key idea: bubbling by neighbour swaps, selecting a minimum, inserting into a sorted part, or merging sorted halves.

### Solution

Finding the minimum of the unsorted part and placing it next in position is **selection sort**. Bubble sort swaps adjacent pairs, insertion sort inserts each new item into an already sorted part, and merge sort splits the list and merges sorted halves.

enonce_markdown: Bubble sort is used to sort 3, 5, 4, 1, 2 into ascending order, and every swap of two neighbours is counted until the list is sorted. How many swaps are made in total?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Each swap of two neighbouring values removes exactly one inversion, that is, one pair that is in the wrong order. The number of swaps therefore equals the number of inversions.

### Solution

The pairs in the wrong order are (3,1), (3,2), (5,4), (5,1), (5,2), (4,1), (4,2): **7** inversions, hence 7 swaps (a simulation confirms it). The value 10 is the number of comparisons of a version without an early stop (4 + 3 + 2 + 1), 5 is the number of items, and 14 counts two assignments per swap.

enonce_markdown: A company in Douala must sort a file of 200 000 customer records. Which statement about the choice of algorithm is correct?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Compare the growth of the running time with the size n: bubble sort and insertion sort are O(n squared) in the worst case, merge sort is O(n log n).

### Solution

For n = 200 000, n squared is about 4 x 10^10 steps while n log n is only about 3.5 x 10^6 steps, so a merge sort is far faster. Bubble sort does not make fewer comparisons on large unsorted data, and the algorithms do not share the same running time. Insertion sort needs many comparisons and shifts on unsorted data. The correct statement is that **merge sort is preferable because its running time grows as n log n, against n squared for bubble sort**.

choix.texte: Bubble sort is preferable because it makes fewer comparisons than merge sort on large unsorted data.
Merge sort is preferable because its running time grows as n log n, against n squared for bubble sort.
All three algorithms take the same time, so the choice only depends on the programmer's preference.
Insertion sort is preferable because it needs no comparisons when the data are unsorted.

enonce_markdown:
The list 29, 10, 14, 37, 13 is sorted into ascending order with selection sort.

(a) Write the contents of the list after each pass. (4 marks)

(b) State how many comparisons are made in the first pass and say whether the number of comparisons depends on the initial order of the data. (2 marks)
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In pass k, selection sort scans the unsorted part to find its smallest item, then swaps it with the item in position k.

### Solution

**(a)**

| Pass | Minimum found in position | List after the pass |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | 10, 29, 14, 37, 13 |
| 2 | 5 | 10, 13, 14, 37, 29 |
| 3 | 3 | 10, 13, 14, 37, 29 |
| 4 | 5 | 10, 13, 14, 29, 37 |

The sorted list is 10, 13, 14, 29, 37 (verified by a simulation).

**(b)** The first pass compares the minimum with the 4 other items: **4 comparisons**. The scan always covers the whole unsorted part, so the total, 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 comparisons, does **not** depend on the initial order (unlike bubble sort with an early stop).

enonce_markdown:
The following Python program sorts a list. Each execution of the loop body that contains `lst[k + 1] = lst[k]` moves one item one place to the right.

```python
def arrange(lst):
    moves = 0
    for p in range(1, len(lst)):
        key = lst[p]
        k = p - 1
        while k >= 0 and lst[k] > key:
            lst[k + 1] = lst[k]
            k -= 1
            moves += 1
        lst[k + 1] = key
    return moves

data = [4, 7, 2, 9, 1, 5]
print(arrange(data), data)
```

What is the first value printed by the last line, that is, how many times is this loop body executed in total?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

This is insertion sort. Each shift removes one inversion (a larger value standing before a smaller one), so the number of shifts equals the number of inversions of the original list.

### Solution

For 4, 7, 2, 9, 1, 5 the inversions are (4,2), (4,1), (7,2), (7,1), (7,5), (2,1), (9,1), (9,5): **8**. Running the program prints `8 [1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9]`. The value 5 is the number of passes of the outer loop, 6 the number of items, and 15 the number of pairs in the list (the worst case, a reversed list).
